what_it_does: Running a very large AI language model — the kind with 50 to 100 billion learned parameters — on a phone or laptop is currently impractical because the model's billions of numbers must be streamed from storage into the processor fast enough to generate each word in real time, and flash storage (the chips that hold data even when the power is off) cannot deliver data quickly enough through its normal interface. Lincoln is a hardware-software co-design that attacks this problem from two angles. When the device is generating the initial response (the compute-heavy phase where it processes your prompt), it repurposes the fast memory interface — the same high-speed electrical connection normally used for the device's main working memory — to move model weights from flash to the processor much faster than the usual storage connector allows. When the device is generating one word at a time (the slower streaming phase), Lincoln instead moves the math computation down onto the flash chip itself, right next to where the data lives, so the numbers never need to travel over the slow link at all. Together, these two ideas let a consumer device run models previously thought to require a data-center server.
